chunks: And from his sermon (peace be upon him) on discouraging [people] from the world.

The world is the house of one who does not criticize it except a wise man, and the house of one who does not understand it except a fool, and the house of one who does not remain in it except a deceived one, and the house of one who does not leave it except a perishing one. It is a dwelling of permanence for one who has no permanence, and a dwelling of transience for one who has no transience. It is a dwelling of action without reward, and a dwelling of planting without harvest. It is a dwelling of change and alteration, and the changing of things one after another, and the changing of the living one after another. It is a dwelling in which transience has preceded, and permanence has lagged behind, and death has preceded, and life has lagged behind. It is a dwelling in which God has made transience a permanence, and permanence a transience, and has made death its end, and life its beginning. It is a dwelling in which God has made action little, and reward abundant, and has made death its end, and life its beginning. It is a dwelling in which God has made transience a permanence, and permanence a transience, and has made death its end, and life its beginning.

key_terms.عَاقِلٌ: Wise man / one of sound intellect

ai.seo_question: How does Imam Ali describe the nature of the world as a place of transience and deception?
ai.summary: In this sermon from *Nahj al-Balagha*, Imam Ali (AS) employs the concept of *Zuhd* (asceticism) not as mere renunciation, but as a cognitive shift to view the world as a transient bridge rather than a permanent abode. This teaching aligns with the Shia scholarly tradition of balancing worldly engagement with spiritual detachment, urging believers to prioritize the eternal *Akhirah* over fleeting material gains. The emphasis on death as a 'brief beginning' underscores the continuity of existence beyond the grave, a core tenet in Shia eschatology.
